passage:
Athletics coach's note, college ground, Saturday
Chandrika has been furious since her relay partner told the selectors she'd "slacked" in practice, which cost her the state trip. On Monday she told me she'd thought of posting the partner's old message screenshots online. She didn't.
What I've seen since: every evening she runs four extra laps, hard, then sits on the bench writing in a small notebook she keeps in her bag. She told me it's where she writes the things she'd like to shout. On Wednesday I saw her talking for a long time with Kishore from the hockey team, who mostly nodded. Yesterday she laughed at practice for the first time in two weeks. Her times have also improved.
What I did next: I told her that her anger made complete sense, and that I was glad she was letting it out on the track and in the notebook rather than online. I've put her name forward for the next trials.

qa.q: How many extra laps does Chandrika run each evening?
qa.a: She runs four extra laps, hard, every evening.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling after her partner's words to the selectors?
qa.a: Chandrika felt furious and hurt, angry enough to think of posting the partner's old messages online.

qa.q: Which of Chandrika's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Writing in a private notebook, talking to Kishore and running hard let her feel the anger safely, so it didn't become a post that would cause new harm.

qa.q: How might Kishore experience these long talks?
qa.a: Kishore may feel trusted and glad to help simply by listening, even without giving advice.

grounding: Shows a young adult letting anger be felt safely through private writing, a trusted friend and hard exercise instead of acting on revenge.

subtype: Stage 5: Deciding to release the grudge [Response]
passage:
First Sunday: Mehak had waited two years for Farida to say sorry for the lie that ended their friendship and cost Mehak the flat they were meant to share. That morning, Farida posted wedding photos. Mehak felt the old heat rise in her chest and realised she was still carrying all of it.
Wednesday: at her small desk after work, Mehak wrote a letter she never meant to send. She wrote everything: the lie, the flat, the loneliness afterwards. Four pages. Then one line at the end: "I'm putting this down now, for me."
The next Saturday: she told her sister about it over chai. "She still hasn't apologised. She probably never will." Her sister asked if that bothered her. Mehak thought for a moment. "It does. But I don't want to wait for her forever." She folded the letter into the back of an old diary. Her chest felt quiet.

qa.q: How many pages was Mehak's letter?
qa.a: It was four pages.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when she saw Farida's wedding photos?
qa.a: Mehak felt the old heat of resentment rise in her chest, and realised with some dismay that she was still carrying the hurt.

qa.q: Why was writing the unsent letter a useful choice for Mehak?
qa.a: It let her say everything fully without needing Farida's reply, so she could choose to put the resentment down for her own peace.

qa.q: What would change if Mehak waited for an apology before letting go?
qa.a: She might carry the resentment for years, since she believes Farida probably never will apologise.

grounding: Shows a person choosing to release a grudge for her own peace through an unsent letter, without waiting for an apology.

passage: Shalini met Chinmay at a café in Koramangala for the first time in a year. He had spread the rumour at their office that she'd been fired for cheating, when in fact she'd resigned. Last month he had messaged her a long apology, admitting he'd been jealous. Today he said it again, face to face, looking at the table. Shalini listened. She had already decided, walking there, that she forgave him; carrying the anger had worn her out. But forgiving him didn't mean telling him things again the way she used to. "I accept your apology," she said. "I'm happy to meet for coffee now and then. I'm not ready to talk about work or my personal life with you yet." Chinmay nodded slowly. "That's fair." They talked about films for twenty minutes. Walking back, Shalini felt lighter, and also clear about where the door was.

qa.q: What rumour had Chinmay spread about Shalini?
qa.a: He had spread the rumour at their office that she'd been fired for cheating.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel walking back from the café?
qa.a: Shalini felt lighter and calm, relieved of the anger but also clear about the limits she had set.

qa.q: Why is Shalini's choice a wise one at this stage?
qa.a: She forgives Chinmay but rebuilds trust slowly, meeting for coffee while keeping work and personal life private until his remorse is proven over time.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel when Shalini sets her limits?
qa.a: Chinmay may feel a little disappointed but also relieved and grateful that she accepted his apology at all.

grounding: Shows a person forgiving without returning to the old trust, choosing limited contact and slow rebuilding based on the other's remorse.

passage: "Pema, you look like you haven't slept. Sit with Naveen Uncle for a minute. When I was twenty-five and a new shift manager at the textile mill, I made a young worker, Somu, stay to finish an order though he told me his mother was ill. She got worse that night, and he wasn't there. She recovered, thank God, but he wouldn't look at me after that. For a year I punished myself. I skipped the Diwali party, I couldn't enjoy anything. One day my own manager said, 'Your guilt is useful only if it changes something.' So I went to Somu's house and said sorry, plainly, no excuses. I changed the rule so anyone with a family emergency could leave, no questions. Then I made myself stop the punishment. I still remember it. But remembering and punishing are different things, Pema. Tell me what's troubling you."

qa.q: What was Somu's mother's condition that night?
qa.a: She got worse that night, and Somu wasn't there, though she later recovered.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel during the year after the incident?
qa.a: Naveen felt guilty and ashamed, punishing himself by skipping the Diwali party and unable to enjoy anything.

qa.q: In the story, which choice turned guilt into repair?
qa.a: After his manager's words, Naveen apologised plainly to Somu and changed the rule for family emergencies, then allowed himself to stop punishing himself.

qa.q: How might Somu have felt when Naveen came to his house to apologise?
qa.a: Somu may have felt surprised and perhaps a little respected, since a manager admitted the wrong plainly with no excuses.

grounding: Shows a person owning harm they caused, apologising and making practical amends, and then allowing themselves to grow instead of endless self-punishment.

passage: The college auditorium had been decorated with the old batch photo blown up huge on the stage, and Kishore stood under it holding a paper cup of juice. Five years since graduation. Around him, the talk moved fast. Hansa had just come back from a master's in Berlin. Two friends had a startup with an office. Someone showed wedding photos, someone else a new car key. "And you, Kishore? Still at the bank branch?" Hansa asked, kindly enough. "Yes," he said, and heard how small it sounded. A month ago he'd been proud of his promotion to assistant manager. Now it felt like standing still while everyone else ran. He laughed at the right moments and clapped for the slideshow, but his chest felt tight. On the drive home, he didn't turn the radio on.

qa.q: Where had Hansa just come back from?
qa.a: Hansa had just come back from a master's in Berlin.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when he answered Hansa's question?
qa.a: Kishore felt small and suddenly behind, with a tight chest, although he had been proud of his promotion a month ago.

qa.q: What could help Kishore after this reunion?
qa.a: He could remind himself what he valued about his own path and talk honestly with a friend, remembering that a reunion shows others' highlights, not their whole lives.

qa.q: How might Hansa have meant the question about the bank branch?
qa.a: Hansa probably meant it kindly, as simple catching up, without realising how it landed after all the talk of degrees and startups.

grounding: Shows a young adult at a reunion suddenly seeing peers with degrees abroad, startups and weddings, and feeling his own path look small and late.

subtype: Stage 2: Counting the roads not taken [Actor]
passage:
Monday: after Sachin's gig at the café, Madhav lay awake making a list on his phone. Things I didn't do. One: music college in Chennai, the audition he'd passed at eighteen and never took up, because Appa said engineers eat and musicians starve. Two: Nisha, who'd moved to Mumbai, and whom he'd never told how he felt.
Thursday: at lunch in the office canteen, he added a third: the year after college he'd spent preparing for an exam he didn't even want. He read the list three times, feeling sick.
The next Monday: Sachin called to ask why he'd left the gig early. Madhav admitted, "Watching you play, I kept thinking, that could have been me. And I didn't even choose not to. I just did what I was told, or what felt safe." Sachin was quiet, then said, "You still play, though. Your guitar's in the corner of your room."

qa.q: What did Appa say about engineers and musicians?
qa.a: Appa said engineers eat and musicians starve.

qa.q: Why does the list make Madhav feel sick?
qa.a: Madhav feels sharp regret and sadness, because the lost chances were shaped by family pressure and fear rather than his own wishes.

qa.q: What could Madhav try next with the list?
qa.a: He could look at which items are still open, like playing the guitar in his room again, and talk them through with Sachin instead of only replaying them.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel hearing Madhav's admission?
qa.a: Sachin may feel a little guilty that his gig stirred this up, but also caring enough to point out that Madhav still plays.

grounding: Shows a young adult listing lost chances, with regret sharpened by choices shaped by family pressure and fear rather than desire.

passage:
Note from the counsellor, company wellbeing programme, second session with Mohit
Mohit arrived early and talked fast. His cousin Anirban, a year younger, got engaged last week, and at the function three aunties asked Mohit when his turn was. His mother has started sending him profiles every evening. He listed his "deadlines": married by 27, own flat by 28, manager by 30. He said, "I'm already late for all of them." When I asked who set those dates, he paused. "Everyone. It's just how it's done in our community." He tapped his foot through the whole session. He said he has not been sleeping well and checks his colleagues' profiles every night.
What I did next: I asked him to write down which of those goals he actually wants and when, separately from what others expect. We talked about how people in his own office are marrying and settling at very different ages. He will bring the list next week.

qa.q: What did Mohit say his deadline was for being married?
qa.a: He said married by 27.

qa.q: How does Mohit feel about his deadlines?
qa.a: Mohit feels anxious and afraid of failing, tapping his foot and losing sleep because he believes he is already late for all of them.

qa.q: What turning point did the counsellor offer?
qa.a: The counsellor asked Mohit to separate what he truly wants from what others expect, and pointed out that people settle at very different ages.

qa.q: How might Mohit's mother see the profiles she sends each evening?
qa.a: His mother probably sees them as caring help and a normal family duty, not realising they add to Mohit's fear of falling behind.

grounding: Shows a young adult feeling time running out under community pressure to marry, earn and settle by fixed deadlines, making normal variation feel like failure.

passage: It was a grey Tuesday in Busan, and Jin sat at his desk at the shipping company staring at the same spreadsheet he'd stared at for three years. On his lunch break he opened a flight site and looked at one-way tickets to Lisbon. He drafted a resignation email and saved it. Walking back from the convenience store, he thought about Selin, how they'd been together four years and still talked mostly about groceries, and he pictured telling her tonight that it was over. The thought felt thrilling for a moment, like opening a window in a hot room. Then, on the subway home, it felt terrifying. He didn't know if he wanted to leave Selin, or Busan, or just the spreadsheet. He only knew he couldn't breathe properly in his life right now, and that everything seemed to need changing at once.

qa.q: How long had Jin been staring at the same spreadsheet?
qa.a: He had stared at it for three years.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Jin have about quitting and leaving?
qa.a: Jin feels restless and trapped, briefly thrilled by the idea of escape, then terrified on the subway home.

qa.q: What could Jin try before making a big move?
qa.a: He could ask what exactly feels missing, talk honestly with Selin, and try one small change, rather than quitting, leaving and breaking up overnight.

qa.q: How might Selin be affected if Jin announced the break-up tonight?
qa.a: Selin would likely be shocked and hurt, since Selin may not know that Jin has been feeling so trapped.

grounding: Shows a young adult having sudden thoughts of quitting, leaving the city and ending a relationship, a signal of unmet needs that impulsive moves may not meet.

passage: In the town of Palani, Ganga was sorting jasmine for the evening temple garlands when her son Kiran came home early from the bank and announced, "Amma, I'm quitting. I want to go to Bengaluru and start something. Anything." Her hands stopped. Her first thought was the loan on the house, the neighbours, his father's old warning. She almost said, "Have you gone mad?" Instead she pushed a heap of flowers towards him. "Help me string these. Then tell me what's missing." Kiran sat down, surprised. As they worked, it came out: every day was the same counter, the same forms. He missed making things, the way he'd built radios as a boy. Ganga listened. "What if you tried something small first? Weekends, a course, a little repair stall at the Thursday market?" Kiran looked at the garland in his hands. "Maybe," he said. "Maybe that."

qa.q: What was Ganga sorting when Kiran came home early?
qa.a: She was sorting jasmine for the evening temple garlands.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when Kiran announced he was quitting?
qa.a: Ganga felt a jolt of alarm and fear, thinking of the house loan, the neighbours and his father's warning, before choosing to stay calm.

qa.q: Why was Ganga's response helpful at this stage?
qa.a: By asking what was missing and suggesting small tests like a weekend course or a repair stall, she treated Kiran's restlessness as information rather than a crisis.

qa.q: What was it like for Kiran when his mother pushed the flowers towards him?
qa.a: Kiran was surprised, having expected an argument, and felt safe enough to explain that he missed making things.

grounding: Shows a parent hearing a restless declaration, resisting panic, asking what is missing and helping test small changes.

passage:
Saturday: Devika spread a sheet of chart paper on Sunaina's floor. "Everything I regret. Go." They wrote it all: the design course she hadn't taken, the friend she'd hurt in college, the years she'd let her uncle choose her job, the city she hadn't moved to.
The next Wednesday: Sunaina drew two columns. "Can still do something" and "Can't change." Devika moved the design course and the friend to the first column. The lost years went to the second. She cried a little over that one.
Two Sundays later: Sunaina asked a new question. "Forget what you're supposed to want. What do you actually care about?" Devika was quiet for a long time. "Making things people use. Being honest with people I love." She circled the design course. That night she messaged the friend from college: "I've been thinking about what I said in second year. I'm sorry." And she signed up for an evening class.

qa.q: What were the headings of Sunaina's two columns?
qa.a: Can still do something and Can't change.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when she put the lost years in the second column?
qa.a: Devika felt sad, crying a little, as she accepted that those years could not be changed.

qa.q: How did sorting her regrets help Devika find a direction?
qa.a: Separating what she could still fix from what she couldn't, and naming her real values, turned vague dread into concrete steps like the apology and the evening class.

qa.q: How might the friend from college feel receiving Devika's message?
qa.a: The friend may feel surprised and touched to get a sincere apology after years, perhaps opening a chance to reconnect.

grounding: Shows a person separating fixable regrets from unchangeable ones and asking what she truly values, which turns dread into a direction.
